prompt.context: Your client is a large toy manufacturer named Marlin (think of a company such as Hasbro or Mattel) with $3B in sales. They are interested in potentially acquiring a smaller company named Dolphin which sells educational toys. Dolphin is different from Marlin since it employs a direct selling model. They hire independent contractors (ICs) to sell their toys for them: these ICs find people to hold parties for them, and invite about 8-10 people whom they sell these toys to. The ICs are paid 20% commission. If the ICs refer a friend to sell Dolphin products and does so, that sale still generates 20% commission for the new IC, but also an additional, smaller commission for the person who originally referred him. This process continues and you get an increasingly smaller cut of sales from members that were referred by those you referred, etc. This downstream sums up to approximately 10% commission total. Dolphin has been losing revenues lately. Two years ago, they had $35M in revenue, one year ago they had $28M, and this year they have $20M. This year they are operating at zero profitability — breakeven. Although the cost of the acquisition is not significant due to their relative sizes, Marlin wants to have a company that can pay its own way.
prompt.question: Two questions: 1. What do both parties have to gain from this acquisition? 2. Why is Dolphin losing revenues and what can it do about it?

clarifying_info.q: What is the growth rate of the educational toy market?
clarifying_info.a: The educational toy market is growing at a rate of 3%; the overall toy market is flat.

clarifying_info.q: Is Dolphin the only company using direct sales in educational toys?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, Dolphin is the only company currently selling educational toys with a direct sales method.

clarifying_info.q: Have any new competitors entered the educational toy space recently?
clarifying_info.a: There were no recent competitor entries in educational toys.

clarifying_info.q: How are other educational toys sold?
clarifying_info.a: Other educational toys are sold through retailers such as Target and Walmart.

clarifying_info.q: Does Marlin currently sell educational toys?
clarifying_info.a: Marlin does not have any educational toys now, but other large toy manufacturers do.

clarifying_info.q: What is the average revenue per party and trend in number of ICs?
clarifying_info.a: Average party revenue has remained constant at $200. The number of ICs has been declining at a rate of 10%. Dolphin is proactively adding ICs, but more are leaving than joining.

clarifying_info.q: What is the industry benchmark for IC compensation?
clarifying_info.a: Industry average for similar job functions is 30% commission with party revenue of $300, yielding $90 per party. Dolphin currently pays 20% on $200 average party revenue, yielding $40 per party.
COGS = 50% of revenue, Fixed Costs = 20% of revenue, Selling Cost = IC commission rate + downstream commission rate (currently 20% + 10% = 30% of revenue).

framework: Question 1 — Acquisition synergies: (a) Revenue synergies for Dolphin and for Marlin, (b) Cost synergies, (c) Marlin's strategic position, (d) Educational toy industry attractiveness

Question 2 — Root cause of revenue decline: (a) External factors (market, competition, demand) vs. internal factors (pricing, product, distribution/sales force), (b) Price decline vs. quantity decline breakdown
Prioritization: Question 2 is higher priority — Marlin wants a company that can pay its own way, so fixing Dolphin's revenue decline is more pressing than synergy enumeration

questions.prompt: Why is Dolphin losing revenue, and what is the root cause?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify the revenue decline is internal/distribution-driven, not external. The educational toy market is growing at 3% and Dolphin products are in high demand. Revenue = number of ICs x parties per IC x revenue per party. Revenue per party is constant at $200. IC count is falling 10%/year, but total revenue is falling faster (~20-28%/year), so each IC must also be holding fewer parties. Root cause: IC compensation ($40/party) is far below industry benchmark ($90/party), so ICs prefer competitors. The number of parties held per IC is declining because the incentive is insufficient.

math.setup: Revenue decline analysis: Year -2=$35M, Year -1=$28M, Year 0=$20M. YoY decline: 35->28 = -20%, 28->20 = -28.6%. IC count falling 10%/year. Revenue per party constant at $200. Therefore parties-per-IC must also be declining. Benchmark: IC earns $40/party at Dolphin (20% x $200) vs. $90/party at competitors (30% x $300).
steps: IC count decline accounts for only 10% per year; remaining decline attributable to fewer parties per IC
Dolphin pays less than half the competitor rate per party
math.answer: Revenue is declining faster than IC count alone can explain. Each IC is also holding fewer parties because Dolphin's $40/party compensation is far below the $90/party industry benchmark, causing ICs to prefer competitors.

questions.prompt: Management proposes raising IC commission to 30% (keeping downstream at 10%). They believe this will double the number of parties. Will this solve Dolphin's profitability problem? (Current cost structure: COGS=50%, Fixed Costs=20%, Selling Cost=commission+downstream.)
questions.guidance: Candidate should build a before/after P&L table. Key insight: raising commission from 20% to 30% increases selling costs by 10 percentage points. Doubling parties doubles revenue AND doubles variable costs (COGS and commissions), while fixed costs stay flat. The math shows profitability remains zero. Candidate should also note that $60/party (30% x $200) is still well below the $90/party benchmark, so doubling parties is an aggressive assumption. The proposal does not solve the problem.

math.setup: Current state: Revenue=$20M, COGS=50%=$10M, Fixed Costs=20%=$4M, Selling Cost=(20%IC+10%downstream)=30%=$6M, Total Costs=$20M, Profit=$0. Proposed state: Commission raised to 30% IC + 10% downstream = 40% total selling cost; parties double so revenue doubles to $40M.
steps: New IC earnings: 30% x $200 = $60/party, still below $90/party benchmark
math.answer: Profitability remains at zero even after doubling parties. The 10pp increase in commission is exactly offset by the revenue doubling's proportional cost increase. The proposal does not solve the problem, and the doubling assumption is likely aggressive since $60/party still trails the $90/party benchmark.

questions.prompt: Revisiting Question 1: How can Marlin and Dolphin help each other, particularly given Dolphin's distribution problem?
questions.guidance: Revenue synergies: Dolphin can leverage Marlin's existing retail distribution channels (Target, Walmart) since its products are in high demand but poorly distributed. Marlin gains entry into the growing educational toy segment and can cross-sell to Dolphin's customer base. Cost synergies: similar physical materials enable economies of scale in raw material procurement, shared manufacturing facilities, and streamlined operations.

brainstorming.prompt: Why might each IC hold fewer parties than before?

categories.name: Compensation / Incentives
ideas: IC commission ($40/party) is far below competitor rate ($90/party)
Diminishing returns on downstream commission make it less attractive
No performance bonuses or tiered rewards for high-volume ICs

categories.name: Competing Opportunities
ideas: ICs pursue multiple direct-selling jobs and allocate time to higher-paying alternatives
Competitors offering 30% commission on $300 average parties are more attractive
Rising gig economy alternatives (rideshare, delivery) compete for IC time

categories.name: Operational / Logistics
ideas: Difficulty finding willing hosts in already-saturated local social networks
Geographic market saturation limiting new party locations
Lack of marketing support or leads from Dolphin to help ICs find hosts

recommendation: No formal recommendation was required for this case; the case concludes after the synergy discussion

If pressed: Marlin should proceed with the acquisition, but must first fix Dolphin's distribution model — either by substantially raising IC commissions above the $90/party benchmark or by expanding into retail channels leveraging Marlin's existing relationships
risks: Commission increase alone does not restore profitability at the current revenue base
Doubling parties is an aggressive assumption given $60/party still trails benchmark
Integration of a direct-selling model into a traditional manufacturing company may create cultural and operational friction
next_steps: Model impact of commission rates above 30% on profitability break-even
Pilot Dolphin products in select Marlin retail partner stores to test incremental demand
Conduct IC exit interviews to validate compensation as primary churn driver
